entries.title: Jordan says its military struck 'militant hideouts' in Syria after deadly church attack
entries.summary: Jordanian armed forces carried out strikes on "militant hideouts" in Syria that it said were linked to a deadly church attack on the kingdom last week. Syria gave a different account.
entries.content:
October 26, 2026

Jordanian armed forces carried out strikes on "militant hideouts" in Syria that it said were linked to a deadly church attack on the kingdom last week. Syria gave a different account.

Jordan said late Monday that its air force has struck military hideouts in southern Syria after determining that suspects linked to last week's deadly church attack were hiding there.

Jordanian forces said the deadly attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church was linked to "terrorist groups" hiding in Syria.

Jordan's armed forces said the strikes on southeastern Syria was carried out in coordination with Damascus.

But Syria gave a different account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks.

A health official told Syria's state news agency that at least five civilians, including women and children, were killed as a result of strikes carried out by Jordan, Reuters reported.

Jordanian security forces arrest 3 men in Karak province

Jordanian security forces earlier on Monday morning arrested three men in connection with last week's deadly terrorist attack at the Hammoud Church that killed nine people and injured 40 others.

Officials said the arrests took place following a dawn shootout with the armed men who were discovered hiding in an abandoned house in the Karak governorate, located some 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.

All three suspects were wounded in the operation, but  Jordanian security forces reported no casualties.

"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," said Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya in a phone interview with state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka on Monday.

"[The suspects] put up fierce resistance but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."

He added that there were "three individuals involved" who were "identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident" and that the security services had "employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."

Jordan's King Abdullah called for 'iron first' response

King Abdullah II of Jordan had ordered authorities to respond with an "iron fist" against anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he added in a statement on Monday, following the arrests, which relatives of the victims had said brought some relief.

"Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs," one relative, himself a survivor of the attack, told Al-Mamlaka.

Who carried out the attack in Jordan?

There has been no claim of responsibility for Friday's deadly attack and Jordan's Public Security Directorate has not named the suspects or publicly ​identified possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.

Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable Middle Eastern state which is a close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: UN sounds the alarm over Israel's West Bank military operation
entries.summary: The UN has sounded the alarm on Israeli action in the West Bank city of Hebron after hundreds of families were displaced at the weekend. Israel has ordered the military to demolish homes after soldiers were killed there.
entries.content:
Israel

UN sounds the alarm over Israel's West Bank military operation

October 26, 2026

The UN has sounded the alarm on Israeli action in the West Bank city of Hebron after hundreds of families were displaced at the weekend. Israel has ordered the military to demolish homes after soldiers were killed there.

The Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron was met with sharp criticism from the head of the UN as well as the UN's human rights commissioner in comments made on Monday.

The criticism comes after an Israeli military operation was launched in the occupied West Bank in response to a shootout on Friday that left two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian gunmen dead. Three more Israeli soldiers were also injured.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the military to demolish buildings in the West Bank city of Hebron and to close off the West Bank. It came just days before Israel's general election on Tuesday.

What did the UN say about Israeli operation in the West Bank?

The United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that "settlements are expanding, evictions are unrelenting with Palestinians driven from their lands," in a post on X.

"We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment, with the spectre of ethnic cleaning looming ever larger," he wrote.

The UN Human Rights High Commissioner Volker Türk also issued a statement condemning Israeli actions, saying the "aggressive operation" has resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely."

"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing," he said.

A UN report, also released on Monday, that accuses Israel of committing war crimes in the West Bank, was rejected by the Israeli Foreign Ministry as "propaganda."

The ministry said that the findings were "not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens."

What is the Israeli operation in the West Bank?

Israeli troops entered the Deir Baha neighborhood, where the assailants lived, and ordered residents to pack up and leave.

The Hebron municipality said that more than 3,000 people, including 200 babies, were ordered to leave.

The Israeli military said at the weekend that its troops were carrying out precise, targeted and thorough searches to "locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure and locate weapons, alongside questioning suspects" in Hebron.

The military said the operation was expected to continue "for several days" and would focus on Deir Baha.

The largescale response to the firefight in the West Bank comes in the run-up to elections in Israel on Tuesday that could bring an end to Netanyahu's premiership.

Netanyahu has frequently painted himself as the only person who can keep Israel safe but his opponents have accused him of lacking a plan.

Edited by: Alex Berry

entries.title: A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
entries.summary: The recent announcement that Syrian tertiary institutes will not allow women into some courses has triggered debate. Critics worry it may be a sign that the new Syrian government is restricting women's rights.
entries.content:
October 26, 2026

The recent announcement that Syrian tertiary institutes will not allow women into some courses has triggered debate. Critics worry it may be a sign that the new Syrian government is restricting women's rights.

Recent changes to university admissions rules in Syria have put a dent in Lin Najab's plans. The 23-year-old from Damascus is one of the few women at her college studying mechatronics engineering.

"My original plan was to pursue a master's degree," Najab told DW. But earlier in October, new rules were announced by Syria's education ministry regarding two newly created colleges, the National University of Defense Sciences and the Syrian University for Security Sciences. The former now restricts certain courses exclusively to male students, and the latter almost all of them.

These new policies could derail Najab's plans. "Now I have to start thinking about other options," she explained. "For example, I might have to move to another province to study."

It is still possible for Syrian women to study the subjects offered by the two new security institutes, but only at other more generalist universities or colleges.

Moving to another province, away from family, brings other difficulties, Najab continued. Student accommodation in dormitories is uncomfortable, but a woman living alone is still frowned upon by conservative Syrians.

"Even if a girl decides she won't give up and wants to go study outside her province, her parents will be opposed to the idea, either for security reasons or because we simply don't want our daughters to go study somewhere else," said Najab.

Controversial ban

The decision to ban women from courses at the new defense and security-related colleges has caused controversy both inside and outside the country.

"Gender doesn't define ability. It should be about high academic standards, the ones I'm trying to meet," Najab argued. "In Syria, we need better education and good graduates, so let's see where the best people are, regardless of gender."

Fatoun Kharbatli, an activist from Aleppo, is also opposed to the idea of limiting certain subjects to one gender. "A person should choose the field in which they see their abilities as lying," she told DW. "We were oppressed for 60 years, so now let's be a nation that keeps pace with global civilization, but without straying from respect and from the basics of our religion.

Qamar al-Yaser, a mother of three in rural Damascus, believes the ban is justified.

The sectors from which women have been excluded "require a strong physique, they need big efforts, travel, organization out in the field and may require staying overnight at remote work sites," said al-Yaser. "These conditions suit young men more than women."

A closer look at some of new admission rules indicate they may be less about restricting Syrian women from certain studies and more about keeping them out of the army. For example, attending the National University of Defense Sciences requires that students serve in the Syrian military. Graduates of the University for Security Sciences must also commit to serving up to 20 years with the internal security forces.

Bad omen?

Does this mean Syria's new government is heading in an increasingly restrictive direction when it comes to women's rights?

Human Rights Watch believes so. A few days after the admissions announcement, the organization released a statement criticizing it. "The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria's international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women's role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes," the organization said.  

Besides the military college bans, there were also other, possibly even more disturbing aspects to the new admissions rules. Restrictions on female students were also applied at a railways institute in Aleppo, oil and gas training organizations in Rmeilan, Homs, Deir el-Zour and Baniyas, and a radio and television course in Idlib. Elsewhere men were barred from kindergarten and nursing school training and midwifery courses. These were to be women-only.

All these come on top of a number of other concerning restrictions and worrying comments by officials. The most recent incident in the education sector involved the government's alteration of school textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year.

The education ministry had already announced it would be removing images and symbols associated with the previous authoritarian regime headed by dictator Bashar Assad. But this week journalists also noticed other changes: Pictures of females in the textbooks who had uncovered hair had been removed, or altered so they were now wearing headscarves. A bare-chested statue pictured in one textbook was now wearing a vest. A picture of men dancing was also gone. 

Common attitudes towards female soldiers

Officials have said that some of the gender-exclusionary rules implemented at the new security institutes were actually carried over from the Assad-era colleges that were fused together to create them earlier this year.

Opposition to female soldiers and military leaders isn't an uncommon attitude in the Middle East's more conservative circles either. Although many Arab countries allow women to attend military colleges and serve, females are often restricted to non-combat or symbolic roles, a 2024 study by the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Institute, or MEI, reported.

In Syria, while women have historically participated in the security services, it was "in a limited and largely symbolic capacity," the Syrian Center for Defense and Security Studies confirmed in a policy paper this year.

But just because an idea is widespread obviously doesn't make it right, human rights advocates have said.

Gender stereotypes

"Gender diversity in the security sector allows all citizens of a country to be perceived as equal in all aspects of their duties and obligations to the nation state, including defending it," Dina Arakji, author of the MEI study, argued. "Allowing women to join the military … can advance a society's perspective on females in nontraditional gender-based roles."

The admissions ban gives young Syrian women a message about what they can and cannot do, Syrian activist Rana al-Ash argued in a commentary about the ban for Paris-based organization, the Syrian Women's Political Movement. 

"When these messages are reflected in admission requirements, confronting familial and societal expectations becomes even more difficult because the educational institution endorses them," al-Ash argued.

For Nadra Bunni, a Syrian analyst at the Middle East Institute Switzerland, it's still unclear as to whether "gender-based restrictions will become a feature of the new Syria."

But the anger over the admissions ban also raises another important question, she noted. "Will Syria's new authorities institutionalize an expectation that government decisions can be questioned and potentially reversed," she asked in a commentary for the online publication, Syria In Transition. "Or [will they] teach citizens that their voices carry little consequence?"

Edited by: R. Casey

entries.title: AI company Anthropic files its IPO in hopes of raising $100 billion
entries.summary: Anthropic has filed paperwork for an initial public offering that could be one of the biggest in history. The company has yet to turn a profit.
entries.content:
October 26, 2026

Anthropic has filed paperwork for an initial public offering that could be one of the biggest in history. The company has yet to turn a profit.

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic on Monday filed paperwork to make its stock market debut in what analysts say could be one of the biggest in history.

The initial public offering (IPO) could happen as early as November, reports say, with analysts putting the company at a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

What did the Anthropic founders say about the IPO?

The seven co-founders of the company, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, outlined their vision for the future of AI in a letter to potential investors.

"We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," they said.

The AI startup behind Claude also addressed the societal risks of AI as they have done before, writing that the company's leadership might have to take unusual decisions to slow down the pace of development, even if that meant falling behind competitors.

The filing toward an IPO represents a major milestone for a company that was founded just five years ago.

Money raised at the IPO could provide the company with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion.

What do we know about Anthropic's IPO?

Anthropic is set to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."

But the company is yet to disclose how many shares it plans to sell and what price, leaving that space blank in its paperwork filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday.

Anthropic filed confidentially with the SEC in June and that gave the agency time to go over the company's financial credentials before they were made available to the public and potential investors.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters.

Anthropic debut follows SpaceX IPO

The San Francisco-based company was founded by members who defected from OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, in 2021.

OpenAI, Anthropic's main rival, is also set to debut on the stock market next year.

Both IPOs are taking place amid growing concern about AI and the race to develop AI infrastructure, including data centers that consume vast amounts of energy.

The document filed by Anthropic shows that the company has seen massive revenue growth but is yet to turn a profit, much like its AI rivals.

Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.

Despite the losses, the company said that it had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of June 30.

And as for money raised at the IPO, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by Elon Musk's SpaceX that ultimately raised $86 billion in what was the biggest IPO on record to date.

Edited by: Alex Berry

entries.title: German police probe cruise ship captain after Bremerhaven collision
entries.summary: A three-ship collision has led to the cancellation of a cruise and expensive damages. Shipyard repairs are needed, and further cruises could be affected.
entries.content:
Germany

German police probe cruise ship captain after Bremerhaven collision

October 26, 2026

A three-ship collision has led to the cancellation of a cruise and expensive damages. Shipyard repairs are needed, and further cruises could be affected.

German police are investigating the captain of the Mein Schiff 3 cruise liner after it collided with two container ships in Bremerhaven.

The collision caused damage estimated to  be in the millions of euros and forced the cancellation of a 20-day Canary Islands cruise, with further voyages potentially affected.

Why are police investigating the captain?

A police spokesperson said proceedings over a possible administrative offense had been opened to establish whether the captain breached his duty of care. Police have not specified the suspected lapse.

Broadcaster RTL reported that investigators spoke to the captains of all three vessels overnight into Monday.

How did the collision happen?

Tugboats were helping the nearly fully booked cruise ship leave the northern German port on Sunday evening when a gust of wind pushed it toward two moored container ships, police said.

The liner was carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members. Nobody was injured, and none of the vessels took on water.

The larger container ship suffered substantial damage, with several meters of its port side torn open and container guides deformed. The smaller vessel sustained minor damage.

The cruise ship was also significantly damaged. Photographs showed damage to its lifeboats and bridge.

All damage was several meters above the waterline. The liner returned to the cruise terminal after the collision.

Could more cruises be canceled?

Technical experts boarded the ship shortly after the accident and determined that shipyard repairs were necessary, operator TUI Cruises said.

The company called canceling the Canary Islands voyage "the only responsible decision," saying passenger and crew safety had "highest priority." Passengers were initially allowed to remain aboard while the company arranged assistance.

It remained unclear whether other voyages planned for this year could go ahead.

The collision initially caused no disruption to other harbor traffic.

Edited by: Alex Berry

entries.title: What Germany thinks of carmaker Audi's $4 billion deal with Trump
entries.summary: The luxury carmaker is set to open its first factory in the United States — a move Trump credits to his tariffs. DW examines the German reaction amid a massive auto industry cull at home.
entries.content:
October 26, 2026

The luxury carmaker is set to open its first factory in the United States — a move Trump credits to his tariffs. DW examines the German reaction amid a massive auto industry cull at home.

1. What is Audi's $4 billion US investment plan?

US President Donald Trump announced the investment on Saturday, during a campaign rally in Georgia, a key battleground state for his Republican Party in the midterm elections next week.

Audi quickly confirmed the plan, saying it would build its first US factory near Macon, Georgia, costing around $4 billion (€3.6 billion) and creating some 4,500 jobs.

The German automaker said construction would begin next year, with a planned annual production of up to 200,000 vehicles due to start in the early 2030s.

The firm plans to build premium SUVs for the US market at the plant, marking a "long-term commitment" to what it said was "one of the world's most important premium markets."

The US investment comes as German automakers face unprecedented pressure from China, rising costs and two conflicts.

Backed by huge government subsidies, Chinese rivals have stolen a march in the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), scaling up production of new models that are fast gaining market share in a crowded global auto market.

BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi's parent company, Volkswagen— the world's second-largest automaker — have all issued profit warnings in recent months as margins come under pressure.

They've also announced major cost-cutting. VW is preparing to axe up to 100,000 jobs by 2030, while Audi's factory in Neckarsulm, which has around 15,000 staff, is one of four plants at risk of closure.

2. Why is Audi investing in US car production?

Trump credited his 15% tariffs on European-made vehicles for Audi's investment, saying it "would not have happened without tariffs."

While the commitment does feed into Trump's plan to bring manufacturing back to the United States from abroad, Audi said it was making the huge outlay for growth and resilience.

“We have much greater ambitions for Audi in America," said the carmaker's CEO Gernot Döllner, who appeared alongside Trump at the Republican's campaign rally.

"The United States is one of the world's most important premium markets, and we have not yet realized our full potential. We are determined to change that ... This is about building a stronger Audi business in America — not only about building a factory," he said.

However, Trump's tariffs have undoubtedly added to the automaker's woes.

Audi, which currently exports to the US market from Europe and Mexico, said the additional costs amounted to about €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) last year.

With more than 160,000 vehicles sold, Audi's US sales last year fell 16%, amid intense competition and after Trump scrapped subsidies on electric vehicles in its second-biggest market.

By building a US factory, Audi should be able to avoid or reduce Trump's tariffs, industry analysts say.

3. What is the reaction in Germany amid huge cuts in the domestic auto sector?

There's been fierce criticism of the deal due to the severe pressure facing German automakers and because the new US investment could mean further job losses at home.

Much of the criticism focused on Döllner's rally appearance alongside Trump.

The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)'s transport policy spokesperson Isabel Cademartori described it as campaign assistance for an autocrat who is waging a trade war against Germany.

"This is a disgrace, especially considering the history of the Volkswagen Group," she stated, referring to the party's links with Adolf Hitler's Nazi party during World War II.

Christiane Benner, president of the powerful IG Metall union, labeled the rally appearance as "extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and not worthy of the company."

VW works council chief Daniela Cavallo went further, saying Döllner had let himself be turned "into a puppet in [Trump's] propaganda show."

Cavallo, however, noted that the US plant could make sense from a business perspective, as VW needs to grow its market share there.

An Audi spokesperson defended the US investment, saying it was "not a decision against Germany, but rather a step toward strengthening our global competitiveness."

Manfred Döss, chairman of Audi's supervisory board, insisted the automaker's future cannot be secured by cost-cutting and efficiency alone.

"We need the courage to invest, to seize new opportunities and to make decisions that will shape our company for decades to come," he added.

4. Will Audi's investment help Trump in the US midterms?

The announcement certainly appears timed to coincide with the US midterm elections on November 3.

Voters will decide whether the Republicans or Democrats hold the balance of power in Congress during Trump's last two years in office.

Holding the announcement in the key battleground state of Georgia is seen as a strategic move to boost the fortunes of local Republican candidates.

Since he returned to the White House last year, Trump has used tariffs and political pressure to force global automakers to relocate their factories to American soil.

Audi's investment follows moves by Stellantis and Japan's Toyota to expand US production, while Honda is in talks to build a new US plant.

US auto giants General Motors and Ford have also promised to increase domestic production.

While one investment announcement may not be enough to sway many voters, it serves one of Trump's main election promises — to revive industrial production in the US.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

entries.title: Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win
entries.summary: Brazilian President Lula secured a surprise win over far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Brazil

Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win

Published October 25, 2026last updated October 26, 2026

Brazilian President Lula secured a surprise win over far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro

  • It was a tight runoff, with Lula winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, official results showed

  • In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race

  • Bolsonaro refused to concede, called for election results to be annulled

  • Trading was suspended on the stock market for half an hour on Monday morning as shares and Brazil's real currency tumbled

  • Several Latin American leaders congratulated Lula on win

  • Germany's Merz said he looks forward to 'deepening strategic ties' with Brazil

  • US President Trump said the vote 'looked terrible,' but added, 'I like Lula'

Keep reading for the latest updates from the second round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 25, with continued coverage into Monday, October 26.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Trump says Brazil vote 'looked terrible to me' but adds, 'I like Lula'

Trump says Brazil vote 'looked terrible to me' but adds, 'I like Lula'

Ask, and you shall receive — sometimes anyway! Now a senior US government representative has commented on Brazil's vote.

Leaving Washington for a midterm election campaign rally, President Donald Trump told reporters that it "looked terrible" to him. 

"I didn't take sides but it looked like another rigged election frankly... it looked so corrupt, so terrible," he said.

Asked by a reporter if he wanted to "do something about the election," Trump seemed to suggest he did not, albeit repeating his criticism of the mechanics of the vote.

"Well, I'm not running Brazil. I'm running the USA. I just thought that the election was, uh — I like Lula, I get along with him very well — I just think it had a very bad look, the election. The way it was tabulated, you know? The extension given was very strange."

Skip next section US yet to comment on Brazil election

US yet to comment on Brazil election

As of 3:20 p.m. in Washington D.C. (1920 GMT), the upper echelons of US government were yet to respond to the election in Brazil on Sunday.

The only October 26 State Department press releases concerned Austria's national day and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's planned trip to Georgia later in the week for a G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting.

Rubio had not opined on his social media channels and US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account — which only tends to pick up on stories with a tape delay unless they involve Trump directly — had remained inactive since Sunday night.

Lula and his Workers' Party often had strained relations with US governments, especially Republican ones, but this has been particularly pronounced in Trump's case.

Skip next section Recap — Why is Bolsonaro crying foul after the voting extension?

Recap — Why is Bolsonaro crying foul after the voting extension?

Just joining us and wondering how Brazil's runoff vote had a considerably clearer margin of victory than predicted and yet still ended in controversy and the losing candidate refusing to concede defeat? 

Challenger Flavio Bolsonaro's objections were focused around the evening extension of voting past the planned closing time of 5 p.m. across the country.

The decisions by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice on Sunday followed a complaint over allegations of pro-Bolsonaro mayors being behind public transport irregularities that may have hampered people's plans to vote.

On election night, Bolsonaro then told journalists it was "impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded."

For now it's unclear whether, as the dust settles, Bolsonaro will continue to resist the outcome and try to encourage protests in the way his now-jailed father Jair Bolsonaro did four years ago.

But two factors in particular seem to speak against the prospects of a potential Bolsonaro challenge.

Firstly, his fairly sizeable margin of defeat — losing by slightly more than 4 million votes rather than just a few thousand — makes it much more unlikely that a two-hour extension at polling stations could have even the theoretical potential of swaying the result.

And beyond that, his camp appealed for and successfully secured permission to keep polling stations open in some of Bolsonaro's southern strongholds, after torrential rains interfered with would-be voters' travel plans.

Skip next section African leaders congratulate Lula, seek to 'advance shared interests'

African leaders congratulate Lula, seek to 'advance shared interests'

Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was one of several African leaders to congratulate Lula on Monday, saying that his renewed mandate offered an opportunity to strengthen bilateral ties. 

"As two leading nations of the Global South, we can promote economic integration and advance our shared interests in a rapidly changing global order," Tinubu said online, saying he looked forward to expanding cooperation in a raft of areas.

Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu also extended her "sincere congratulations" to Lula. 

"Tanzania values its longstanding friendship with Brazil, and looks forward to continue building on this foundation to further strengthen bilateral relations and deepen cooperation, for the mutual benefit of our two nations," Suluhu said.

Seychelles President Patrick Herminie called the runoff election result "a powerful affirmation of the trust the Brazilian people have placed in President Lula's leadership," in comments published by his office online. 

He said Lula's win was "a testament to his lifelong commitment to the dignity and well-being of ordinary men and women," saying the Seychelles shared Lula's values like "social justice, equality of opportunity, the protection of workers and the most vulnerable, and a model of development that places people at its center."

Herminie expressed a desire to deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in tackling climate change, protecting the oceans and advancing the interests of the Global South.

Skip next section Putin congratulates Lula, praising his 'personal contribution' to bilateral ties

Putin congratulates Lula, praising his 'personal contribution' to bilateral ties

Russian President Vladimir Putin offered congratulations to Lula in a telegram published by the Kremlin on Monday. 

"It is difficult to overstate your personal contribution to strengthening the strategic partnership between Brazil and Russia," the telegram stated.

Putin, a leader of a fellow BRICS alliance member, is one of few world leaders to have worked with Lula across all of his presidential terms, starting in 2003. 

Putin also congratulated Lula on his upcoming 81st birthday, which falls on Tuesday.

The Russian president's spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow earlier in the day that the Kremlin welcomed Lula's re-election.

Skip next section WATCH: Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results

WATCH: Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a historic fourth term after defeating far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro in a runoff election.

It's a historic political comeback for Lula who trailed in the first round.

DW reports from Rio de Janeiro.

Skip next section Sao Paulo stock exchange halts trading over sharp drop after Lula win

Sao Paulo stock exchange halts trading over sharp drop after Lula win

Trading on the Sao Paulo stock exchange, the largest in Latin America, was suspended for 30 minutes on Monday after plummeting nearly 17% in the wake of the re-election of left-wing Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who defeated conservative Flavio Bolsonaro.

The sharp drop in the benchmark Ibovespa index triggered a 30-minute "circuit breaker" mechanism provided for "periods of sharp market decline," according to a stock exchange statement.

Meanwhile, the US dollar surged 12% against Brazil's currency, one of the real's biggest ‌daily moves on record.

Prices of raw sugar, one of Brazil's most important exports, slid nearly 5% on the collapsing exchange rate.

Prediction markets had indicated a Bolsonaro win but the right-wing senator's refusal to concede defeat and ​his pledge to challenge the election result have added to investor uncertainty.

"Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result, or at least allows the constitution to run its course," Chris Turner, a strategist at ING in London, told the Reuters news agency as attention turned to Lula's choice of finance minister — a clue as to his fiscal approach.

"The key signal for markets will ⁠be the ​next Lula administration's commitment to fiscal discipline, starting with the appointment of a new finance minister in coming weeks," RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Graham ​Stock told Reuters.

Skip next section Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil

Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders  congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.

"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.

Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.

Skip next section Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win

Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win

Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index ‌Bovespa ⁠falling ⁠nearly 15% in early Monday ​trading 

On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.

Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.

Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.

Skip next section Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election

Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election

The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.

"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

He said Russia hoped for more of the same.

Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.

However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.

Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.

It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.

Skip next section Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close

Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close

Here's a DW infographic on where the results stand:

Skip next section France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory

France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory

Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.

China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."

Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."

French President Emmanuel Macron, after expressing his congratulations, said Brazil and France should work to "strengthen our strategic partnership."

"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."

Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, was more effusive, casting Lula's victory as evidence that the world is experiencing a backlash to its seeming rightwards political trajectory at present.

"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.

Skip next section Big challenges face Lula's fourth term

Big challenges face Lula's fourth term

Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is likely to face several difficulties in enacting his agenda in a fourth-term.

 Among other things, Brazil has elected its most conservative congress since the country's return to democracy in the 1980s.

Flavio Bolsonaro's ​Liberal Party and allies could control more than 280 seats in the 513-seat lower ⁠house and up to 50 seats in the 81-seat Senate following parliamentary elections three weeks ago.

This could lead to Lula's being forced to cede to congress on decisions about the budget, important legislation and key nominations.

Economic woes

Brazil is also in a period of weak economic growth, with his government forecasting just a 2.3% rise in GDP next year.

This is combined with public debt that surpasses 82% of GDP, the highest rate since the coronavirus pandemic.

Security concerns

Public security also remains a major concern in Brazil, with criminal organizations holding considerable influence in parts of the country.

Lula has said he plans to establish a Ministry of Public Security to combat the problem.

Environmental problems

There are also environmental challenges ahead.

Although deforestation in the Amazon — a major carbon sink and thus vital for the stability of the world climate — fell significantly during Lula's third term, Brazil is still a long way from its goal of ending deforestation by 2030.

Skip next section EU's von der Leyen hails Lula's win

EU's von der Leyen hails Lula's win

The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, has posted an online message of congratulation to "my friend" Lula on his win in Brazil's election runoff. 

"Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil," she wrote.

"Europe's partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come," her post continued.

"Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate."

Skip next section Could Bolsonaro succeed in annulling the vote?

Could Bolsonaro succeed in annulling the vote?

Some uncertainty still surrounds the final result of Brazil's election, as Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to challenge the outcome over the two-hour extension of polling hours ordered by a Supreme Court judge at the request of Lula da Silva's campaign.

However, legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether such a complaint would meet the legal threshold for the election to be annulled.

Bolsonaro's case would be weakened by at least two factors, analysts said. Firstly, the scale of his loss to Lula and second, the fact that his campaign had also requested an extension in some states.

The president of the electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, said that the extension of voting hours had not influenced the vote.

The Associated Press cited Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at Brazil's Fluminense Federal University, as saying that Bolsonaro could ask for the elections to be declared null and void by filing a complaint with electoral authorities or the Supreme Court.

"But there isn't much legal basis for that," Padua said.

"The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters' ability to freely express their will. There doesn't seem to have been any such impact," he said.

Shortly before scheduled voting ended, Supreme Court Judge Christiano had ordered polling stations to remain open for longer after problems with public transport were reported to be affecting voters.

The decision followed a request from Lula's campaign.

Bolsonaro's campaign had also called for an extension of voting hours but only in some conservative-leaning southern states hit by heavy rainfall, flooding and power outages that were said to be disrupting voting.

entries.title: Why Ukraine may be involved in Mali's conflict
entries.summary: Allegations that Ukrainian specialists are supporting Tuareg rebels in Mali highlight Kyiv's effort to challenge Russian influence far beyond the battlefield in Europe.
entries.content:
Mali

Why Ukraine may be involved in Mali's conflict

October 26, 2026

Allegations that Ukrainian specialists are supporting Tuareg rebels in Mali highlight Kyiv's effort to challenge Russian influence far beyond the battlefield in Europe.

Ukraine is fighting Russia — and the conflict may extend into Africa's Sahel region.

According to an investigation published by US media outlet CNN in September, around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are reportedly supporting Tuareg rebels in northern Mali. Their common enemy: the military government in Bamako and its Russian allies.

But how reliable is the information? And what price could Kyiv pay for engaging in Africa?

Marta Oliynyk-D'omochko, coordinator of the African Studies Program at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, sees a strategic motive. "Ukraine's main interest is to weaken Russia's influence around the world," she told DW. If Russia's military influence were rolled back, she added, the economic opportunities arising from it would also diminish.

Russian historian Irina Filatova, professor emeritus at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, also considers Ukrainian support for the Tuareg movement plausible. However, she said she has no independent evidence to confirm such involvement.

Kyiv's alleged partners are controversial. The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) cooperates with the Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated with al-Qaeda.

Suspicions dating back to 2024

In July 2024, DW reported on possible involvement by the Ukrainian military intelligence service (HUR) in an ambush on Russian Wagner fighters near Tinzaouaten in northern Mali.

At the time, HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov said the Tuareg rebels had received information they needed to carry out the attack. Ukraine denied direct involvement.

Paramilitaries from Russia's Wagner Group and Malian troops suffered heavy losses in the July 2024 attack. 

CNN's investigation has reignited the question of whether the Russia-Ukraine war is also being fought on African soil.

Signals from Kyiv, but no confirmation

The suspicions were renewed by a post on X by Kyrylo Budanov. The former head of Ukraine's military intelligence, now chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on September 7 that Ukrainian intelligence protects the country's interests worldwide — "from Russia to Africa … in the burning desert sands and in the snows of icy Antarctica...".

Budanov did not explicitly mention Mali and his post does not confirm any specific operation. CNN reported that the Ukrainians provided drone training, operational planning and remote support for drone missions. DW has not independently verified those claims.

DW reached out to the HUR for comment. Among other things, DW wanted to know whether personnel had been deployed to Mali, whether the political leadership had approved such a mission, and what measures were in place to ensure that the JNIM — which cooperates with the FLA — does not indirectly benefit from Ukrainian support.

DW did not receive a specific response. An HUR spokesperson said the agency might provide information at a later date. The extent of any potential Ukrainian involvement therefore remains unclear.

Why Mali matters to Kyiv

Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Mali increasingly turned away from Western partners and toward Russia. The Wagner Group was subsequently replaced by the Africa Corps in 2025 as Moscow reorganized its military presence.

Russia has sought to consolidate its influence in the Sahel region and present itself as a reliable security partner.

Ulf Laessing, former head of the Sahel program of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Mali and now head of its Syria and Iraq program, said Russia is continuing to expand its activities in Africa.

"I have received information that the Africa Corps still uses Syria and Libya as transit points for flights from Russia, including for refueling and loading, to support its operations on the continent," Laessing told DW.

From Ukraine's perspective, it could be attractive to exert pressure on Russian forces in Africa.

Filatova sees a strategic logic to this: "The Ukrainians regard Russian troops anywhere in the world as legitimate targets." Setbacks in Mali could tie up Russian resources and undermine Moscow's reputation as a security partner, she argued.

However, Oliynyk-D'omochko stressed that the relationship with the Tuareg is not a comprehensive alliance. The FLA is not seeking to replace the government in Bamako. Instead, it is focused on northern Mali and is pursuing self-determination or extensive autonomy.

Oliynyk-D'omochko describes the relationship as a tactical arrangement: "It is more of a situational alliance against a common enemy than a comprehensive partnership."

The alliance with jihadists

The FLA is fighting for an independent state in the north of Mali, a region predominantly inhabited by Tuaregs. JNIM, by contrast, aims to impose strict Islamic rule. Both groups oppose the military government and its Russian allies, but their objectives differ.

Any potential Ukrainian support for the FLA would not, in itself, prove that Kyiv is directly supporting JNIM. However, jihadists could benefit indirectly if they conduct joint operations with FLA or gain access to knowledge and equipment.

Cooperation between Tuareg and Islamist groups dates back more than a decade.

After the ousting and killing of Libya's longtime dictator Muammar al-Gaddafi during the Arab Spring in October 2011, heavily armed Tuareg fighters returned to Mali and took up the struggle for an independent state.

In the process, separatist ambitions became intertwined with Islamist movements. Iyad Ag Ghaly, the current leader of JNIM, was himself involved in the Tuareg rebellion before turning to jihadism.

According to Oliynyk-D'omochko, the cooperation is primarily tactical in nature. The two sides have collaborated during past uprisings but later fell out. It remains unclear how long the current alliance will last.

For Kyiv, this also poses a political risk. In many African countries, the Tuaregs are viewed as separatists. Cooperation with them could therefore create the impression that Ukraine is interfering in another country's internal affairs.

Claims of support for armed groups

Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso accuse Ukraine of supporting armed groups and threatening their territorial integrity. The three Sahel nations, all ruled by military governments, have severed diplomatic relations with Kyiv and deepened their cooperation with Russia.

In September, Mali's Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop accused Ukraine at the United Nations of "providing clear and open support to terrorist groups and other mafia-like groups to undermine our country's territorial integrity," reported Agence France-Presse. Diop did not provide evidence for his claim.

The three nations' governments have may have an interest in legitimizing their partnership with Moscow and portraying Kyiv as a destabilizing actor.

Oliynyk-D'omochko has found no definitive proof of the allegations, yet warned of the potential consequences for Ukraine's Africa policy. Kyiv advocates equal partnerships with African countries. Any alleged cooperation with separatists could undermine that message and affect how potential partners view Ukraine.

What price could Ukraine pay?

Engagement in Mali could offer Ukraine a relatively low-cost way to weaken Russian interests beyond Europe. A small team of specialists could train local fighters and improve their capabilities in the use of drones.

But a potential partnership with the FLA carries political risks. Because the Tuareg separatists cooperate with the JNIM, Kyiv could face accusations of indirectly supporting jihadist fighters. That could undermine Ukraine's efforts to strengthen its relations with African countries.

This article has been translated from German



Correction, October 26, 2026: An earlier version of this article stated that the CNN investigation was published in October 2026; the report was published in September. DW apologizes for the error.

entries.title: Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests that rocked France
entries.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron said his government will announce "strong measures" in response to violent protests in France in recent weeks. But he also acknowledged that students have "legitimate" grievances.
entries.content:
France

Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests that rocked France

October 26, 2026

French President Emmanuel Macron said his government will announce "strong measures" in response to violent protests in France in recent weeks. But he also acknowledged that students have "legitimate" grievances.

The French government is set to announce a series of "strong measures" to assuage protests which have rocked France in recent weeks, President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.

Speaking in the southern city of Marseille, Macron warned that fresh demonstrations planned for this coming Saturday were "risky" and said that protest routes would remain outside city centers in order to protect public order.

France braces for 'lively' Halloween

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told broadcaster BFM that he was expecting further disturbances on October 31.

"Halloween evening is traditionally always a bit lively," he said. "We expect it to be complicated again."

Prior to Macron's arrival in Marseille, the Elysee Palace said the president intended to "pay tribute to and thank the internal security forces that helped restore republican order" in France's second-largest city where protesters briefly stormed the city hall on October 17.

He acknowledged that French authorities had "not anticipated at all" the scale of demonstrations which descended into widespread violence in looting in several major cities, leading to suggestions the state had lost control of the streets.

Macron: 'Social media is damaging our democracies'

The French president also highlighted the role of social media in the protests, saying the online networks were "damaging our democracies" by "bringing young and not-so-young people to places where criminal acts, attacks and looting were taking place."

He described social media as "tools for mobilizing the worst impulses."

While Macron admitted that French security forces underestimated the extent to which "extreme left forces" would meet up "so early in the day" on October 17, Interior Minister Nunez highlighted the phenomenon of organized far-right mobs confronting left-wing activists in several cities.

"We ​knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out to defend businesses," he told BFM.

"In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organized formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."

A presidential aide said Macron wanted to demonstrate that "the state is present, standing firm and fulfilling its mission to protect."

The president said that curfews enabled relative order to be maintained during last Saturday's protests (October 24), when authorities also deployed 70,000 police officers across the country, making 1,435 arrests.

"The state prevailed this weekend. The state was strong," government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told RTL radio.

France: Macron acknowledges 'legitimate' student demands

Nevertheless, President Macron also said he had instructed his government, led by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, to "respond to the legitimate demands that lie at the root of this social movement."

He said the government will soon announce several "concrete and huge" measures aimed at addressing student concerns over education and university admissions, following a nationwide consultation with high school and university student representatives.

"There are demands that must be heard and answered," confirmed government spokeswoman Bregeon.

"But to answer them, ​there is a prerequisite: a return to calm. We cannot have a functioning social dialogue in a climate of violence such as the one we experienced a week ago."

Edited by: Alex Berry

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Germany's Merz heads to Asia as security issues loom large
entries.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be meeting the leaders of Singapore, Japan and South Korea as Germany seeks to adjust its foreign policy to rising uncertainty and threats to global supply chains.
entries.content:
South Korea

Germany's Merz heads to Asia seeking closer security ties

October 26, 2026

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be meeting the leaders of Singapore, Japan and South Korea as Germany seeks to adjust its foreign policy to rising uncertainty and threats to global supply chains.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz kicked off a five-day tour of Asia on Monday, traveling to Singapore before his scheduled visits to Japan and South Korea. Merz is accompanied by an entourage of 30 senior businesspeople, including representatives of Germany's industry, tech and defense companies, and energy suppliers.

At the same time, Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is visiting China.

While the trips are not officially related, they both seem aimed at boosting Berlin's economic and security relationships at a time of geopolitical instability, which threatens global supply chains.

Japan needs close allies

In Singapore, Merz is set to deliver a major foreign policy speech and meet Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. He will then travel to Japan on Wednesday to meet with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and take part in the German-Japanese Business Summit.

Merz's visit "will be very much welcomed in Tokyo," said Ben Ascione, an assistant professor of politics and international relations at Tokyo's Waseda University.

"For more than a decade, Japan has been looking to generate new security allies and closer trade partnerships," he told DW.

"This greater outreach was started under Prime Minister [Shinzo] Abe, but Takaichi is very much following that blueprint because of the growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific region and the greater uncertainty around the second administration of [US President] Donald Trump," he added.

Germany and Japan face different, but connected threats

The challenges posed by an increasingly expansionist China in the region are of deep concern to Tokyo, particularly as Beijing is forging closer ties with both Russia and the unpredictable regime in North Korea. China and Russia have conducted joint military exercises off Japan, and Beijing is resolute in its insistence that Taiwan be brought under the control of the mainland.

Ascione points out that any conflict over Taiwan, the disputed islands of the South China Sea or territorial claims elsewhere in the region would have a major impact on global trade. Such disruptions would also impact Germany.

"Japan and Germany have different primary security threats at the moment, with Germany focused on the Russian invasion of Ukraine and Japan keeping a close watch on China, North Korea and Russia, but I do believe that Germany has come more into line with Takaichi's perception of the security threat that is posed by China," Ascione said.

"Takaichi is going to underline the importance of a rules-based order and the policy of a free and open Indo-Pacific at a time of such geopolitical uncertainty," he added. "Japan has in recent years moved towards greater resilience building, supply chain resilience and more and deeper security partnerships."

German military assets welcome in Japan

According to Ascione, Japan would also "welcome" Germany deploying its military assets to the region, following its Bayern frigate docking in Tokyo in 2021 and its fighter jets conducting air drills with Japanese fighters in 2024.

The frigate Bayern became the first German Navy warship to dock in Tokyo in 20 years in May 2021 and went on to conduct air and maritime exercises with Japanese units. In July 2024, German Eurofighter Typhoon aircraft similarly carried out air drills with Japanese fighters over northern Japan.

Merz and Takaichi are expected to exchange views on responding to geopolitical threats.

This would include ensuring supply chain resilience, protecting strategically important industries and ensuring access to technologies and components, such as the rare earths that are critical to a range of advanced technologies but remain largely controlled by China.

European nations 'irritated' by Seoul's outreach to North Korea

Merz is then scheduled to visit South Korea, where he will meet with President Lee Jae-myung and open the 19th Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul. He is also due to visit the Demilitarized Zone that marks the border between North and South Korea.

Security issues will again dominate discussions in Seoul, believes Saeme Kim, a research fellow at The Asan Institute for Policy Studies.

However, the German leader could voice concerns about South Korea's perceived "outreach" efforts towards North Korea and, by extension, Russia.

"There has been discussion recently about exports of petroleum to Russia, although Seoul says it has not breached sanctions," she said.

South Korea is trying to set up a way to communicate with Pyongyang, according to the expert, despite the regime of Kim Jong Un sending troops to the conflict in Ukraine.

"It's not just Germany, I think a lot of European countries will be irritated by the Lee administration trying to improve relations with North Korea and Russia," Kim said.

The South also continues to provide humanitarian assistance to North Korea, even as the regime forges ever closer economic ties with China and Russia.

"The government needs to keep in mind that some of these policies are going to be damaging to South Korea's own interests over the long-run," she said.

Can South Korea learn from Germany's history?

At the same time, Merz could also offer insight into two Koreas trying to work with one another, drawing on the German experience of reuniting in 1990.

"There are lessons that South Korea can learn, of course, but there are a lot of differences," Kim said. "The two Koreas are still technically at war and Seoul has to deal with an aspiring nuclear power on its border."

Merz will have the opportunity to see the North at a distance when he visits the DMZ. His visit to the border, however, could also be canceled due to lingering tensions over the North Korean mine injuring three South Korean soldiers last month. Pyongyang has accused the South of staging the incident.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic
